findings.measured: Below 150 Hz the correlation is 0.35; bass and kick may thin out in mono.

steps.text: Add Utility to the track (or the Main track) and turn on Bass Mono at about 120 Hz.

other_options.text: Check the kick and bass tracks for chorus, wideners or stereo patches.

findings.measured: The audio is still loud at the last sample; the ending may be cut off.

steps.text: Extend the Arrangement selection past the last reverb and delay tails, then export again.

other_options.text: Drag a fade-out on the last clip in the Arrangement, then export again.

notes.headline: Solid mix with good headroom — fix the stereo bass and the chopped ending before you send it on.
notes.summary: This bounce is in good shape technically: -13.66 LUFS integrated with -1.06 dBTP true peak leaves plenty of room for mastering, and the channels are balanced within 0.06 dB. Two things need attention. Below 150 Hz your correlation is 0.35, so the kick and bass may thin out when the track collapses to mono, and the file is still loud at the last sample, which means the ending is likely cut off mid-tail.

priorities.title: Bass is too wide below 150 Hz
priorities.why: At 0.35 correlation down low, the kick and bass lose weight anywhere the signal folds to mono — club systems, phone speakers, a lot of streaming playback. It also makes the low end harder for mastering to control.

priorities.title: The ending is cut off
priorities.why: The audio is still loud at the final sample, so reverb and delay tails are being chopped. That reads as a mistake on any playback and leaves mastering nothing to fade.

listen_for: Flip to mono and check whether the kick and 808 hold their weight — compare before and after the Utility Bass Mono setting at 120 Hz.
On a small speaker or phone, listen for the low end disappearing in the busiest section.
Play the last few seconds of the new export and confirm the reverb and delay tails ring out instead of stopping dead.
After bass-monoing, check that the overall width of the track still feels the same up top.
strengths: -13.66 LUFS with -1.06 dBTP true peak and 12.6 dB peak-to-loudness gives mastering plenty of headroom and dynamics to work with.
Left/right balance is 0.06 dB — effectively centered.
Mono loss is only 0.7 dB overall, so the full-band summing is fine; the issue is confined to the low end.

judge.priority_order: Both findings are warnings; F1 (wide low end) is placed first as it has broader audible consequence (mono collapse on many systems) than F2 (ending cut off), a reasonable ordering.
judge.explains_impact: F1's why explains thinning on club/phone/streaming playback and mastering difficulty; F2's why explains chopped tails being audible as a mistake.
judge.groups_causes: F1 and F2 are unrelated causes and are correctly kept as separate priorities, not merged.
judge.specific: Notes reference exact measurements (-13.66 LUFS, -1.06 dBTP, 0.35 correlation, 0.06 dB balance, 120 Hz Utility setting) specific to this bounce.
judge.stage_appropriate: Notes correctly frame the mix as having headroom for mastering and don't judge it against release loudness standards.
judge.faithful: All claims (correlation values, mono loss, true peak, ending issue) match the report; no invented problems or contradictions.
judge.concise: Notes are focused and avoid filler, though the 'listen_for' section adds some extra checks beyond the two findings without becoming bloated.
